metadata.title: Exploring teacher job satisfaction in five Latin American countries: A Multi-level analysis using TALIS 2018
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire micro-data for five Latin American systems (Chile, Argentina/Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, Colombia, Mexico, and Brazil) and applies TALIS sampling weights at both teacher and school levels, together with TALIS replicate weights, to obtain design-consistent variance estimates. The authors report that they could not incorporate stratum weight adjustments because TALIS stratum weights are confidential (OECD, 2019), which may affect precision of variance estimates even though overall weighting and replication are used. The analytic sample is restricted to countries with fully harmonised TALIS 2018 micro-data, weights, and documentation publicly available in the same cycle, and variables with >5% missingness or strong distributional issues (skewness/kurtosis) are excluded prior to modeling. Data preparation was conducted in R (2024.04.1+748) and multilevel estimation was run in Mplus 8.4, with teacher-level predictors group-mean centered and school-level predictors grand-mean centered to support within-school interpretation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample includes TALIS 2018 participants from five Latin American systems only: Chile, Argentina (Autonomous City of Buenos Aires), Colombia, Mexico, and Brazil, because these are the only systems with fully harmonised TALIS 2018 micro-data, weights, and documentation publicly available in the same cycle. Variables were selected based on TALIS 2018 Technical Report guidance and a data quality analysis: variables with missing values above a 5% threshold or exhibiting strong bias (kurtosis and skewness) were excluded. Missing data were handled using Mplus WLSMV with a pairwise-present routine (every teacher–school pair responding to a given item contributes to the covariance matrix), and the authors state all analysis variables had ≤5% non-response. Teacher-level predictors were group-mean centered within schools and school-level predictors were grand-mean centered across the full sample.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (teacher questionnaire) — teacher job satisfaction composite (T3JOBSA)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel WLSMV (Mplus) — country-specific fixed-effect coefficients (γ) with p-values; e.g., Chile: cooperation γ=0.136 (p<.001), self-efficacy γ=0.144 (p<.001), stress γ=-0.378 (p<.001), stakeholders γ=0.509 (p<.001), workload stress not significant; Argentina (CABA): cooperation γ=0.128 (p<.001), self-efficacy γ=0.207 (p<.001), stress γ=-0.306 (p<.001), stakeholders γ=0.451 (p<.001), workload stress not significant; Colombia: cooperation γ=0.057 (p<.01), self-efficacy γ=0.172 (p<.001), stress γ=-0.285 (p<.001), stakeholders γ=0.470 (p<.001), workload stress γ=-0.326 (p<.01); Mexico: cooperation γ=0.086 (p<.001), self-efficacy γ=0.131 (p<.001), stress γ=-0.355 (p<.001), stakeholders γ=0.418 (p<.001), workload stress γ=-0.172 (p<.05); Brazil: cooperation γ=0.092 (p<.001), self-efficacy γ=0.188 (p<.001), stress γ=-0.283 (p<.001), stakeholders γ=0.369 (p<.001), workload stress γ=-0.274 (p<.01). Model fit/explanatory power: R2L1 (teacher level) ranges 0.161–0.269; R2L2 (school level) ranges 0.533–0.755; null model ICC ranges 0.071–0.157 across countries.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire the study leveraged teacher cooperation, teacher self-efficacy, workplace well-being/stress, stakeholder participation, and workload stress to model teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA) in five Latin American countries, finding that cooperation and self-efficacy are consistently positively associated with job satisfaction while workplace stress/well-being is consistently negatively associated. It also finds that stakeholder participation is a strong positive organizational predictor across all countries, and workload stress is a significant negative predictor in most contexts (notably Colombia, Brazil, and Mexico). This indicates that teacher well-being policies should prioritize collaborative professional cultures and self-efficacy supports, alongside workload-stress reduction and participatory school governance, while recognizing that some effects (e.g., workload stress, demographic variables) are context-dependent and the analysis is cross-sectional.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes TALIS 2018 teacher questionnaire data for five Latin American systems (Chile, Argentina/Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, Colombia, Mexico, and Brazil) to explain teacher job satisfaction (T3JOBSA) using a two-level multilevel framework estimated in Mplus with the WLSMV estimator. The authors report country-specific fixed-effect coefficients (γ) and significance levels rather than ML predictive accuracy, with R2L1 (teacher level) ranging from 0.161 to 0.269 and R2L2 (school level) ranging from 0.533 to 0.755. Across countries, teacher cooperation and teacher self-efficacy show positive associations with job satisfaction, while workplace well-being and stress show robust negative associations. At the school level, participation among stakeholders is consistently one of the strongest positive predictors, whereas workload stress is significantly negative in several countries. Limitations include cross-sectional TALIS data (no causal inference) and the inability to use TALIS stratum weights due to confidentiality, which may affect precision of variance estimates.
